newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: FORECAST-Revamp to spur Pick 'n Pay yr shr.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-Revamp to spur Pick 'n Pay yr shr.

text.p: A return to aggressive pricing and marketing, and benefits from a group restructure will help underpin annual earnings growth at South African retailer Pick 'n Pay Stores Ltd, analysts said on Friday.
But they said the expected sturdy 25 percent rise in profits for the year to end-February, due for release on Wednesday, would be coming off a low base after a rough patch in 1995.
"The base is still quite low as they had a terrible year in 1995 when there was a big drop in earnings mainly because of a strike," said John Biccard, an analyst at Smith Borkum Hare.
Analysts said that Pick 'n Pay had in the past year managed to claw back some market share lost to competitors during the labour unrest.
"They have got more aggressive on pricing and refurbished a lot of stores...They are definitely running the business better," Biccard said.
Analysts polled by Reuters forecast Pick 'n Pay's annual earnings per share rising to between 27.4 cents and 29.3 with consensus at 28.2 -- an increase of nearly 25 percent on last year's 22.6 cents.

They expected the dividend to rise to within a band of 15.7 and 17.2 cents with consensus at 16.6. Last year's dividend was 13.5 cents. Figures for 1996 have been restated to take into account the issue of new "N" shares last year.
The reorganisation of the firm 18 months ago into two focussed divisions, retailing and group enterprises, each under their own managing director, was also starting to bear fruit.

"They have got their act together with a much sharper focus, they are gaining market share and margins are on the recovery track...moving Sean Summers to retail was good as he is a better operator," another analyst said.
Since late 1995, Summers has headed the core retailing business under the Pick 'n Pay brand name, while Gareth Ackerman, son of chairman Raymond Ackerman, took charge of all other operations.

Other drivers for growth in the past year included a strong performance from Score Supermarkets, in which Pick 'n Pay owns a 75 percent stake, a recovery in its hypermarket business and the impact of high real interest rates on the group's cash balances.
